relevance_reason: The title says the paper reports a novel CISD2 mutation in Italian siblings with Wolfram syndrome 2. This is direct evidence for the WFS2 entry.

findings.statement: Rondinelli et al. (2015) identified a novel CISD2 mutation in Italian siblings with Wolfram syndrome 2.
quotes: Wolfram syndrome 2: a novel CISD2 mutation identified in Italian siblings.

relevance_reason: Case report of a WFS2 patient with a novel homozygous CISD2 exon 2 deletion, including clinical, platelet and molecular findings.

findings.statement: Mozzillo et al. (2014) reported a 17-year-old Caucasian (Italian) girl born to parents who said they were not consanguineous. She had recurrent bleeding upper intestinal ulcers from age 5 years. At age 14 she was diagnosed with malrotation and partial duodenal intussusception, which required duodenal resection. At 16 she developed reduced visual acuity and dyschromatopsia with optic disc pallor, and at 17 she developed non-autoimmune diabetes requiring insulin. She also had bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and slow intestinal transit with entero-gastric bile reflux.
quotes: Since the age of 5 years old, FS suffered from recurrent b-UIU. When 14 years old, malrotation and partial duodenum intussusception were diagnosed, resection of a duodenal tract and duodenal-jejunal anastomosis were performed.
At 17 years old non-autoimmune diabetes occurred and WFS2 was suspected. She started insulin treatment.
Further examinations showed a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in the high frequencies (SHLHF), and a slow intestinal transit time with entero-gastric bile reflux (EGBR).

findings.statement: In the patient reported by Mozzillo et al. (2014), the eye examination showed slight optic disc pallor with preserved pupillary light reflexes. Pattern VEPs were normal, and brain MRI showed normal optic nerve caliber. Visual field, ERG, microperimetry and OCT testing showed moderate bilateral optic nerve involvement compatible with optic neuropathy, not optic atrophy, and the findings were unchanged after 5 years of follow-up. At age 22 she had optic neuropathy with preserved visual acuity and no optic atrophy. The authors suggested that the ocular disease in the Jordanian WFS2 patients was probably also optic neuropathy, and that WFS2 might not be a true WFS subtype.
quotes: Visual field testing, ERG, MP, and OCT of macula and retinal nerve fiber layer showed a moderate involvement of the optic nerve in both eyes, compatible with a diagnosis of Optic Neuropathy (ON), excluding the OA (Figure 1) and other ocular abnormalities.

Since our patient does not show OA at the age of 22 years, and since “asymptomatic” OA described in Jordanians is not completely supported, we suppose that the ocular pathology in those patients was probably ON and not OA.

findings.statement: Mozzillo et al. (2014) found that their patient had reduced, reversible platelet aggregation in response to ADP at concentrations up to 10 micromolar, with no platelet secretion in response to ADP. Aggregation in response to collagen, epinephrine and ristocetin was normal, and the other main coagulation tests were normal. Her heterozygous parents and brother also showed reversible ADP-induced aggregation defects without clinical signs. The authors suggested that differences in experimental conditions or between patients could explain why the Jordanian patients had a collagen aggregation defect instead.
quotes: Evaluating PA, a reduced and reversible defective PA up to 10 μM of ADP was present, whereas PA in response to other tested agents (collagen, epinephrine, ristocetin) was within normal ranges. Platelet secretion in response to ADP was absent (Figure 2).
Ophtalmological abnormalities, DM and deafness were not found in the parents and brother, whereas a reversible PA in response to ADP was found.

phenotypes.text: absent platelet secretion in response to ADP

findings.statement: In their patient, Mozzillo et al. (2014) found a novel homozygous deletion of all of CISD2 exon 2, detected because exon 2 failed to amplify by PCR and confirmed by cDNA sequencing. SNP array analysis restricted the deletion to at most 2,050 bp, extending from intron 2 to intron 3. Her parents and brother were heterozygous for the deletion. The deleted region includes the codons for amino acids 102 to 106 within the 2Fe-2S domain, and the authors suggested this would result in a nonfunctional protein. Runs-of-homozygosity analysis showed no parental relationship, but microsatellite analysis supported a common ancestor; the grandparents came from the same small Italian island.
quotes: CISD2 cDNA sequencing revealed a novel homozygous deletion affecting the whole exon 2 of CISD2 (see Additional file 1: Figure S1).
The maximum deletion size was restricted to a region of 2,050 bp spanning from intron 2 to intron 3.
The deletion was homozygous in the proband and heterozygous in her parents and brother.

variants.as_reported: homozygous deletion affecting the whole exon 2 of CISD2

relevance_reason: Cisd2 knockout mouse model of WFS2 showing mitochondrial degeneration and premature aging, supporting a mitochondria-mediated pathogenesis.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2009) found that Cisd2 deficiency in mice caused mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction accompanied by autophagic cell death. These events preceded the two earliest signs, nerve and muscle degeneration, and together led to a set of features suggestive of premature aging. Mitochondrial degeneration worsened with age, and autophagy increased alongside the premature aging phenotype.
quotes: Cisd2 deficiency in mice causes mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction accompanied by autophagic cell death, and these events precede the two earliest manifestations of nerve and muscle degeneration; together, they lead to a panel of phenotypic features suggestive of premature aging.
mitochondrial degeneration exacerbates with age, and the autophagy increases in parallel to the development of the premature aging phenotype

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2009) showed that Cisd2 is located mainly in the mitochondria and is involved in controlling mammalian life span.
quotes: Our study also reveals that Cisd2 is primarily localized in the mitochondria
Here we show for the first time that CISD2 is involved in mammalian life-span control.

findings.statement: Chen et al. (2009) concluded that their Cisd2 knockout mouse findings strongly support the hypothesis that Wolfram syndrome is partly a mitochondria-mediated disorder. They proposed that CISD2 mutation causes the mitochondria-mediated disorder WFS2 in humans.
quotes: our Cisd2 knockout mouse work provides strong evidence supporting an earlier clinical hypothesis that WFS is in part a mitochondria-mediated disorder; specifically, we propose that mutation of CISD2 causes the mitochondria-mediated disorder WFS2 in humans.

relevance_reason: Identifies the causative ZCD2 (ERIS/CISD2) mutation in Wolfram syndrome 2 families and characterises the protein's function.

findings.statement: In 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome that had previously been shown not to have WFS1 mutations and that mapped to the WFS2 locus on 4q22-q25, Amr et al. (2007) identified a homozygous G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 of the ZCD2 gene, predicting a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution at a conserved residue. The mutation disrupted mRNA splicing by eliminating exon 2, resulting in a premature stop codon; the authors concluded that the aberrant splicing, rather than the amino acid change, was the basis of pathogenesis.
quotes: A single missense mutation was identified in a novel, highly conserved zinc-finger gene, ZCD2, in three consanguineous families of Jordanian descent with Wolfram syndrome (WFS).
A G-->C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicts an amino acid change from glutamic acid to glutamine (E37Q).
The mutation was found to disrupt messenger RNA splicing by eliminating exon 2, and it results in the introduction of a premature stop codon.

findings.statement: Amr et al. (2007) noted that the 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome lacked WFS1 mutations and had been mapped to the WFS2 locus at chromosome 4q22-q25.
quotes: It had been shown that these families did not have mutations in the WFS1 gene (WFS1) but were mapped to the WFS2 locus at 4q22-25.

findings.statement: Because WFS1 mutations also cause nonsyndromic low-frequency and progressive hearing loss and optic atrophy with hearing loss, Amr et al. (2007) screened 377 probands with hearing loss for mutations in the WFS2 gene and found none.
quotes: Screening of 377 probands with hearing loss did not identify mutations in the WFS2 gene.

findings.statement: Amr et al. (2007) showed that the ZCD2-encoded protein, ERIS (endoplasmic reticulum intermembrane small protein), localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum, like wolframin, but does not interact directly with wolframin.
quotes: The ZCD2-encoded protein, ERIS (endoplasmic reticulum intermembrane small protein), is also shown to localize to the endoplasmic reticulum but does not interact directly with Wolframin.

findings.statement: Amr et al. (2007) found that lymphoblastoid cells from affected individuals with Wolfram syndrome 2 showed a significantly greater rise in intracellular calcium upon thapsigargin stimulation compared with controls, although resting intracellular calcium concentrations did not differ.
quotes: Lymphoblastoid cells from affected individuals show a significantly greater rise in intracellular calcium when stimulated with thapsigargin, compared with controls, although no difference was observed in resting concentrations of intracellular calcium.

relevance_reason: This paper first describes families with Wolfram syndrome linked to 4q22-24, which defines the WFS2 locus.

findings.statement: El-Shanti et al. (2000) studied 16 patients from 4 families with the Wolfram syndrome phenotype who also had features not previously reported. None of the affected family members had diabetes insipidus, and several patients had profound upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.
quotes: To pursue the possibility of locus heterogeneity, 16 patients from four different families were recruited. These patients, who have the Wolfram syndrome phenotype, also have additional features that have not previously been reported.
There is an absence of diabetes insipidus in all affected family members. In addition, several patients have profound upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding.

findings.statement: Using 3 microsatellite markers (D4S432, D4S3023, and D4S2366) linked to the chromosome 4p16.1 Wolfram syndrome locus, El-Shanti et al. (2000) significantly excluded linkage to that locus in 3 of the 4 families. In the other family, the 2 affected individuals were homozygous for all 3 markers from the 4p16.1 region. Homozygosity mapping in the 3 unlinked families showed linkage to chromosome 4q22-24.
quotes: With the use of three microsatellite markers (D4S432, D4S3023, and D4S2366) reported to be linked to the chromosome 4p16.1 locus, we significantly excluded linkage in three of the four families.
The two affected individuals in one family showed homozygosity for all three markers from the region of linkage on chromosome 4p16.1.
For the other three families, genetic heterogeneity for Wolfram syndrome was verified by demonstration of linkage to chromosome 4q22-24.

findings.statement: El-Shanti et al. (2000) reported further evidence of genetic heterogeneity in Wolfram syndrome: 1 family was consistent with the 4p16.1 locus and 3 families linked to 4q22-24. The authors stated that they had identified a new locus that plays a role in the etiology of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.
quotes: provide further evidence for the genetic heterogeneity of this disorder. We also provide data on a new locus that plays a role in the etiology of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.
